plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 5.2.9
plan.contextChunk: This figure contains two panels, (a) and (b), illustrating the disk method for computing the volume of a solid of revolution. Panel (a): the 2D xy-plane showing region R bounded above by the curve y = f(x), below by the x-axis, and between x = a and x = b; a rotation arrow at x = b indicates revolution about the x-axis. Panel (b): a 3D perspective of the resulting solid; at a generic position x along the axis, a circular disk cross-section is highlighted in blue with radius f(x) labeled, showing that each cross-section perpendicular to the x-axis is a disk of area pi[f(x)]^2. The figure derives the disk method formula V = integral from a to b of pi[f(x)]^2 dx by identifying the cross-sectional area at each x and integrating along the axis of revolution.

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: The flat region in panel (a) and the solid in panel (b) are the same object before and after rotation about the x-axis

interactions.label: Function and interval
interactions.teaches: The formula and interval completely determine both the planar region and the solid; at every x, the disk radius is the height f(x)

interactions.label: Cross-section position x
interactions.teaches: Sweeping x through the interval shows that the volume is built from disk slices whose area is pi[f(x)]^2

demo_steps.title: Start with the planar region
demo_steps.narration: The curve y = f(x) bounds the shaded region R above the x-axis from a to b. This is the region that will be revolved.

demo_steps.title: Rotate into a solid
demo_steps.narration: Switching to the solid view shows the result of revolving R about the x-axis. The top and bottom outlines come from the same height f(x).

demo_steps.title: Read one disk slice
demo_steps.narration: At the selected x-value, the highlighted cross-section is a disk. Its radius is f(x), so its area is pi[f(x)]^2.

demo_steps.title: Sweep the disks
demo_steps.narration: Moving the slice from a toward b shows how the disk radius changes along the axis. Integrating these disk areas gives the volume.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Default mathematical setup: f(x)=sqrt(x), a=1, b=5, with x displayed from about 0 to 5.8 and y from about -2.5 to 2.7. Panel (a) is a flat xy-plane: x-axis horizontal left-to-right, y-axis vertical at the left, shaded region R from x=a to x=b under y=f(x), above y=0. Use light blue fill #c8e3ee with about 0.75 opacity, curve stroke bright blue #2aa6d9, boundary strokes dark gray/black #222222, axes black #222222. The curve rises gently from sqrt(1)=1 at a to sqrt(5)=2.236 at b; the label y=f(x) sits above the curve near the upper middle; R is centered inside the shaded area. The rotation arrow is a small gray curved arrow looping around the x-axis just to the right of b. Panel (b) solid: generate surface of revolution around the x-axis with parametric coordinates (x, r cos theta, r sin theta), r=f(x), x in [a,b]. Render in a side-on textbook view with x left-to-right and y vertical, so circular cross-sections appear as vertical ellipses. The left end cap at a is a smaller ellipse, the right end cap at b is a larger ellipse. The top silhouette follows +f(x), the bottom silhouette follows -f(x), with black outlines. The current disk defaults at x=3, radius sqrt(3)=1.732, shown as a vertical light-blue translucent ellipse with a saturated blue rim #2aa6d9, centered on the x-axis. Put a red center point #e94b4b on the axis at the disk center, a small x label below it, and a vertical brace or bracket to the right of the disk labeled f(x). Live readouts should show radius f(x) and area pi[f(x)]^2 using the parsed formula. If bounds are edited, require a<b; dynamically remap the cross-section slider to [a,b]. If f(x) is negative or non-real on part of the interval, show an inline validation warning because the disk-method figure assumes f(x)>=0.
interactionPlan.notes: Use the viewMode toggle instead of showing both textbook panels simultaneously. For the 2D region, sample the parsed function at 150-250 points and build a filled polygon down to the x-axis. For the 3D solid, build a BufferGeometry mesh with roughly 120 samples in x and 48-72 angular samples; use a pale translucent blue material so the disk slice remains visible. Draw silhouettes and end-cap ellipses as separate Line geometries for a textbook-style outline. The cross-section disk should update reactively with both the equation input and x slider; compute displayed area as Math.PI * r * r. Keep labels screen-facing with CSS2D or sprites. Catch parser errors and invalid bounds inline without crashing the scene.

authoredContext:
Let f be continuous and nonnegative on [a, b], and let R be the region that is bounded above by y = f (x), below by the x-axis, and on the sides by the lines x = a and x = b (Figure 5.2.9a). Find the volume of the solid of revolution that is generated by revolving the region R about the x-axis. We can solve this problem by slicing. For this purpose, observe that the cross section
of the solid taken perpendicular to the x-axis at the point x is a circular disk of radius f (x)
(Figure 5.2.9b). The area of this region is
A(x) = π[f (x)]

Because the cross sections are disk shaped, the application of this formula is called the
method of disks

discrepancies: The default curve for y = f(x) is a simple sqrt(x) shape and does not match the source curve's flatter middle with a sharper rise near b.
The source shows panels (a) and (b) side by side, while the generated version uses a toggle so only one panel is visible at a time.
The shaded region in panel (a) has noticeably different proportions, with a much taller vertical edge at b and a more sloped top boundary than the source.
The rotation arrow near b is present but its placement and shape are less like the source's small vertical loop around the x-axis.
The generated figure adds substantial UI, readouts, and editable controls that are pedagogically useful but visually not part of the original static textbook figure.
evaluation.notes: The figure captures the disk-method region and solid well, with useful interactions, but the default function shape and proportions differ from the source.
action_items: Use a default profile curve that more closely matches the source figure, including the flatter middle and sharper rise near b.
Adjust the panel (a) region proportions so the heights at a and b and the curve shape resemble the original more closely.
Refine the rotation arrow near b to match the source's small vertical loop around the x-axis.
Consider adding a side-by-side view option showing panels (a) and (b) simultaneously to better match the textbook layout.
